web.title: Funding for Agricultural Startups in Africa: Grants, Loans, and Investments
web.description:
Outline

This guide walks through where that funding actually sits in 2026: government-backed schemes, development finance institutions, grants for young founders, dedicated funding for women in agriculture, and the venture capital and private investors putting real money into African agritech.

## How Much Venture Capital Is Actually Going Into African Agritech
African agritech startups raised just $200,000 combined in January, an almost negligible sum for a sector this size. February brought $55 million in agritech funding.

Female-founded agritech startups raised 58% of total sector funding that year, up from 51% in 2024, even though they represented a smaller share of total deals.

Debt financing is also becoming a bigger part of the picture across African startups generally, agriculture included. African startups raised a record $1.6 billion in debt in 2025, up 63% year on year, and debt now accounts for 41% of all capital raised on the continent, a trend we cover in more depth in our guide to [seed funding for African startups](https://mohacafrica.org/seed-funding-for-african-startups/). It means lenders are increasingly willing to finance proven business models without demanding equity in return.

## Types of Funding Available to African Agri-Startups
A pre-revenue agritech idea has almost no chance with a venture capital fund looking for traction, but it has a real shot with a grant or accelerator built for early-stage founders.

## Government-Backed and Development Finance Institution Funding
It is a fund-of-funds, meaning it does not lend directly to startups but instead channels catalytic capital into investment vehicles that are active in African agriculture. Through those funds, FASA supports investment ranging from $15,000 to $5 million for growing agri-SMEs across the continent.

South African founders also have access to government grant schemes like CASP and Ilima/Letsema, along with a growing agri-crowdfunding market that has raised more than R50 million for local agricultural startups over the past five years, a sign that retail investors are also willing to back agriculture when given accessible platforms.

## Venture Capital and Private Investors Backing African Agritech
Real deals tell you more about what investors want than any funding list can, so it is worth looking at what actually got funded recently.

Africa Feed & Food closed MAD 850 million, roughly $91.3 million, in March 2026, backed by RNAF III, a North African fund managed by RMBV, alongside development finance institution Proparco.

At the smaller end, Koolboks raised $1.5 million from Cascador to manufacture pay-as-you-go solar freezers for food vendors and farmers, directly addressing the cold-chain gap that causes so much post-harvest loss across the continent. Eja-Ice, backed by Shell-seeded impact investor All On, raised $1 million to build off-grid solar freezers, cold rooms, and cooling tricycles. Investors have clearly noticed, since a large share of 2026’s funded agritech deals in Nigeria alone went to companies building cooling or cooking hardware.

For founders raising funding for agricultural startups in Africa right now, that means researching these specific investors and their portfolio patterns will produce better results than a generic pitch to any fund with “Africa” in its name.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Do women get more funding for agribusiness in Africa?
Female-founded agritech startups raised 58% of total sector equity funding in 2025, up from 51% the year before, and agritech was one of only two sectors, alongside insurtech, to reach full gender parity in equity funding that year.

Nigeria remains one of Africa’s most important markets for agricultural technology, with agritech startups and small businesses attracting between $220 million and $270 million in disclosed funding between 2022 and 2025.

The funding has supported businesses developing technology for agricultural production, supply chains, farmer financing, food distribution and other areas of the agriculture value chain.

According to Disrupt Africa’s _African Tech Startups Funding Report 2022_, Nigerian agritech startups raised $72.77 million in 2022, representing about 55 per cent of the $132.825 million raised by agritech startups across Africa during the year.

The strong performance was largely driven by a major transaction involving Thrive Agric, which raised $56.4 million in debt financing from local commercial banks and institutional investors.

The company also received a $1.75 million co-investment grant from the USAID-funded West Africa Trade & Investment Hub.

Disrupt Africa described the Thrive Agric transaction as one of the largest agritech funding rounds on the continent in 2022.

Thrive Agric and Kenya-based Apollo Agriculture accounted for more than 80 per cent of Africa’s agritech funding that year, showing the extent to which a small number of large transactions influenced the continent’s overall funding figures.

Agritech funding across Africa weakened in 2023, with startups raising $84.64 million, representing a 36.3 per cent decline from the $132.825 million recorded in 2022.

According to Disrupt Africa, only five Nigerian agritech startups raised a combined $6.75 million during the year.

Releaf, an agricultural supply-chain technology company, raised $3.3 million in pre-Series A bridge financing in January 2023, following a $4.2 million seed round in 2021.

However, another industry dataset points to a larger level of investment when the wider agrifoodtech sector is considered.

For MSMEs operating in agriculture, access to funding can provide capital needed to purchase equipment, expand production, improve technology and reach new markets.

For Nigeria, sustained investment in agritech could therefore support not only technology startups but also farmers, processors, distributors and other MSMEs operating across the agricultural value chain.

The funding trend also underscores the importance of creating an environment where agritech businesses can access patient capital, build sustainable business models and scale solutions capable of improving productivity and market access.

web.description:
# Agritech startups receive $220m
![Solution to food insecurity in Nigeria](https://thenationonlineng.net/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/Drone.jpg)

Nigeria remains one of Africa’s most important markets for agricultural technology, with agritech startups and small businesses attracted between $220 million and $270 million in disclosed funding from 2022 through 2025.

Disrupt Africa’s African Tech Startups Funding Report 2022 recorded $72.77 million raised by Nigerian agritech startups, out of $132.825 million raised by the sector across Africa. Nigeria therefore accounted for about 55 per cent of the continent’s agritech funding that year.

The 2022 figure was heavily influenced by a single transaction of Thrive Agric raising $56.4 million in debt financing from local commercial banks and institutional investors, alongside a $1.75 million co-investment grant from the USAID-funded West Africa Trade & Investment Hub.

Disrupt Africa described the transaction as one of the largest agritech funding rounds on the continent that year.

It noted that [Thrive Agric](https://thriveagric.com/) and Kenya’s Apollo Agriculture together accounted for more than 80 per cent of Africa’s agritech funding that year.

Within Nigeria, just five agritech startups raised a combined $6.75 million, according to the same report.

Individual transactions nevertheless continued to emerge. Releaf, an  agricultural supply-chain technology company, raised $3.3 million in pre-Series A bridge financing in January 2023, following a $4.2 million seed round in 2021.

- [Agritech firm, partners unveil facility to boost animal health](https://thenationonlineng.net/agritech-firm-partners-unveil-facility-to-boost-animal-health/)

Only 14 African agritech startups raised funding, compared with 24 in 2023.

AgFunder’s AgriFoodTech Investment Report 2025 recorded $192 million across 91 agrifoodtech deals in Africa in 2024.

Nigeria attracted $26 million, placing it behind Kenya, which received $95 million, while Egypt also recorded $26 million.

According to Briter Intelligence, African agritech funding reached about $483 million in 2022 before falling to $194 million in 2023, recovering slightly to $206.9 million in 2024 and then declining again to $168.1 million in 2025.

This year in May 2026, Sabou Capital announced a $2 million impact-linked debt facility for Tomato Jos Farming and Processing, a Kaduna-based tomato processor. The naira-denominated facility is intended to expand the company’s processing capacity and smallholder farmer network.

AgFunder’s data have placed Nigeria among Africa’s leading agrifoodtech markets, while the country’s large agricultural economy and extensive smallholder farming base continue to attract companies working in agricultural finance, supply chains, processing, market access and climate resilience.
